content: Nasal polyps are a common occurrence in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Sinus infections in these patients have been identified as a contributing factor to the development of severe chest complications. Additionally, the presence of nasal polyps has been associated with an increased risk of lower respiratory tract infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Topical nasal steroids have been proven effective in treating nasal polyps in individuals without cystic fibrosis. However, there is currently no definitive evidence supporting their efficacy in managing nasal polyps in people with cystic fibrosis. This review represents an updated version of a previously published analysis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical nasal steroids in treating symptomatic nasal polyps in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from extensive electronic database searches and manual searches of relevant journals and conference proceedings. The most recent search was performed on June 10, 2015. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the effects of topical nasal steroids to placebo in individuals with cystic fibrosis who had nasal polyps. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted relevant data. Only one single-center trial, involving 46 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared the use of a topical steroid (betamethasone) administered as nasal drops to a placebo. The treatment was given twice daily for six weeks, with 22 participants receiving the active drug. The study evaluated subjective symptom scores, changes in polyp size, and side effects. The results showed no significant difference in nasal symptom scores between the treatment and placebo groups. However, betamethasone was found to be effective in reducing the size of nasal polyps. This benefit was accompanied by an increased incidence of mild side effects, including nasal bleeding and discomfort. The trial had a high risk of bias, as more than 50% of the enrolled participants did not complete the study. Additionally, the short follow-up period of six weeks limited the clinical relevance of the findings. The authors concluded that topical nasal steroids do not appear to have a significant effect on subjective nasal symptom scores in individuals with cystic fibrosis and nasal polyposis. While they may reduce the size of nasal polyps, the evidence supporting their efficacy is limited due to the small sample size, high dropout rates, and lack of long-term follow-up in the included trial. Overall, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of topical nasal steroids for nasal polyps in this population. The authors emphasized the need for a well-designed randomized controlled trial with adequate sample size and long-term follow-up to provide more robust evidence. Such a study should include validated measures of symptoms and physical findings, as well as address quality-of-life outcomes.
